title: Capstone: reconstructing a function you have never seen
objective: By the end of this capstone you can take an unfamiliar function's disassembly and produce a C declaration and body that account for every instruction in it.

blocks.text: This is the whole course applied at once. Below is a real function, compiled from source you have not seen. The task is to work out what it does, what its parameters are, and what data it operates on — using only the instructions.

blocks.caption: Real compiler output, labels renamed for readability

blocks.text: Before reading any instruction in detail, find the structure. The two conditional jumps inside the .L2 block — jne .L5 and je .L5 — target .L5, which sits at a lower address, so they are backward jumps, and a backward jump means a loop. The loop body spans .L5 through the two tests at .L2: the counter is incremented at .L5, and the two jumps back to it are both 'skip to the next iteration'. There are two exits: .L6 reached by the loop finishing or by falling through, and .L7 reached before the loop even starts.

rows: First parameter, a pointer to 16-byte elements
Compared to rcx to end the loop; tested for <= 0 at the start
Starts at 0, incremented once per iteration
The loop index — not a parameter
Set to -1 before the loop, set to ecx on success

blocks.text: That gives the signature almost completely: three parameters in rdi, rsi and edx, returning an int. The jle rather than jbe on rsi says the count is signed, and the 32-bit edx says the third parameter is 4 bytes wide.

blocks.caption: Two instructions define the whole structure
lines: add  rdi, 4                        ; before the loop, bias the pointer
add  rdi, 16                       ; per iteration: element size is 16
cmp  dword ptr [rdi - 4], edx      ; 4 bytes at offset 0 of the element
test byte ptr [rdi], 8             ; 1 byte at offset 4, testing bit 3
/* The +4 bias exists so both accesses can use small displacements. Undo it:
[rdi - 4]  is element offset 0,  read as 4 bytes
[rdi]      is element offset 4,  read as 1 byte
Stride 16, a 4-byte field at 0, a flag byte at 4. */

blocks.title: The pointer bias is a common trick worth recognising
blocks.text: Adding a constant to a pointer before a loop lets the body reach fields on both sides of it with the smallest possible displacements, which produces shorter instructions. When you see a pointer adjusted once before a loop and then indexed with negative displacements inside, undo the bias mentally before reading the offsets — otherwise every field offset you recover will be wrong by exactly that constant.

blocks.caption: What the instructions add up to
lines: uint32_t field_at_0;      /* compared against the third argument */
/* ... 11 more bytes we cannot see, because this function never
touches them; the stride of 16 is how we know they exist */
int mystery(const struct rec *a, long n, uint32_t want) {
struct rec { uint32_t id; uint16_t flags; uint16_t len; const char *name; };
Verified by running the program: sizeof(rec)=16, id@0, flags@4, len@6, name@8.
The reconstruction got the size, both touched offsets and the whole
algorithm right. It could not know about len and name -- because the
function never reads them, and nothing in the code refers to them. */

blocks.title: What the limit of the method is, exactly
blocks.text: The reconstruction recovered everything the function does and nothing it does not. Fields the code never touches are invisible except as the gap the stride implies; whether the flags field is one byte or two cannot be determined from a single byte test; and no name in the result is the real name. That is the honest boundary: disassembly gives you behaviour with complete fidelity and intent not at all. Naming things correctly is the part that requires a hypothesis and evidence from elsewhere — strings, imports, how callers use the result.

items: Find the backward jumps first: those are the loops, and they give you the shape
Identify the exits and what value each returns
Classify the registers: parameters in ABI order, an index, an accumulator, a return value
Note signed versus unsigned from the condition names: jle and jl against jbe and jb
Recover element size from the stride, and field offsets from the displacements
Undo any pointer bias applied before the loop
Read the size annotations for field widths and movsx or movzx for signedness
Write the C, then account for every instruction — an unexplained instruction means the reconstruction is incomplete

blocks.title: The last step is the one people skip
blocks.text: A reconstruction that explains most of the instructions is a guess. Go back and point at each instruction, including the push rbp and the jmp that skips into the middle of the loop, and say why it is there. In the function above, the unconditional jmp .L2 before the loop body exists because the compiler rotated the loop and had to enter it at the test rather than at the increment. If you cannot explain an instruction, you have missed something the function actually does.

items: Write three small functions of your own, compile each at -O1, strip the binaries, and put the source somewhere you will not look at it
Wait a day. Working from the stripped disassembly alone, reconstruct all three using the checklist above
If you have someone to work with, swap binaries instead — but this course assumes you are alone, and waiting a day is a surprisingly good substitute for not knowing the answer
Compare each reconstruction against your original and record exactly what was recoverable
For every difference, decide whether it was unrecoverable in principle or a mistake in method
For a harder version with no source at all, take any small binary from /usr/bin and reconstruct one of its functions

blocks.text: That last distinction is the whole point of the exercise. A field you could not see because the function never touched it is a limit of the evidence. A field offset you got wrong because you forgot a pointer bias is a limit of your method — and the difference between the two is what separates a careful analyst from a confident one.

rows: Whole programs rather than single functions: control-flow graphs, data structures across many functions, and tools that keep your annotations
Looking for the missing bounds check, the signed comparison that should be unsigned, the buffer written past its end
The same reading, plus packing, obfuscation and anti-analysis defences layered on top
Reading what the compiler produced to find out why it is slow, which you have now done repeatedly
The other side of the same material: producing this output rather than reading it

blocks.text: All five start from the same skill you have just demonstrated. The binary is the only account of what a program does that is guaranteed to be accurate, because it is the thing that runs. Everything else — the source, the documentation, the commit message — is a claim about it.

blocks.title: One more, harder
steps: Compile a function containing a switch with eight cases and reconstruct it from the disassembly
Compile one that returns a 32-byte struct and identify the hidden pointer
Compile one taking a mix of integers and doubles and recover the exact signature
Compile a recursive function at -O2 and determine whether it still recurses
Take any function from a system library, disassemble it, and write down what it does
For that library function, check your conclusion against its documented behaviour
Record one thing you got wrong and the instruction that would have told you
blocks.expected: Reconstructions that match, and at least one instructive error. The system-library step is the real test: it is the first time the answer is not something you wrote, and checking your reading against the documented behaviour is the closest thing to a ground truth this work has. Recording the instruction that would have told you is how the next reading gets better.

cheatsheet: Find backward jumps first: they give you the loops and the shape
Classify registers by ABI position: rdi, rsi, rdx, rcx, r8, r9 then index and accumulator
jle and jl mean signed; jbe and jb mean unsigned
Stride gives element size; displacement gives field offset; size annotation gives field width
Undo any pointer bias applied before the loop before reading offsets
In the worked example: stride 16, 4-byte field at 0, flag byte at 4, bit 3 tested
Verified against the source: sizeof 16, id@0, flags@4, len@6, name@8
Fields the function never touches are invisible except as the gap the stride implies
Account for EVERY instruction; an unexplained one means the reconstruction is incomplete
Disassembly gives behaviour with complete fidelity and intent not at all

checkpoint.prompt: A loop body advances rdi by 16 each iteration and reads dword ptr [rdi - 4] and byte ptr [rdi], with rdi having been increased by 4 before the loop. What are the field offsets?
checkpoint.explanation: Undo the bias of 4 that was applied before the loop. The bias exists so both accesses use small displacements, and forgetting to undo it makes every recovered field offset wrong by exactly that constant.

checkpoint.prompt: The loop is bounded by cmp rsi, rcx followed by je, and guarded at the top by test rsi, rsi followed by jle. What does that tell you about the count parameter?

choices.A: Signed — jle is the signed condition
choices.D: Nothing about its type can be recovered

checkpoint.explanation: A negative count is handled by the guard test returning immediately. Signedness is visible in the condition names, not the comparison. jle and jl are signed; jbe and jb are unsigned.

checkpoint.prompt: The reconstruction recovered the element size and two field offsets but not the remaining eleven bytes of the structure. Why?

choices.A: They are in a different section

checkpoint.explanation: Nothing in the code refers to them; their existence is known only from the 16-byte stride. Disassembly gives behaviour with complete fidelity. What the code does not do leaves no trace beyond the space it occupies.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is 'account for every instruction' the step that must not be skipped?

choices.A: To find dead code the compiler failed to remove
choices.D: Explaining most instructions is not enough

checkpoint.explanation: An instruction you cannot explain means the function does something you have not accounted for. In the worked example the unconditional jmp into the middle of the loop is explained by loop rotation. An unexplained instruction is the signal that the reading is incomplete.

checkpoint.prompt: Under the System V AMD64 integer calling convention, what role does edx have on entry to this three-parameter function?

choices.B: It holds the third integer argument
choices.C: It is always the loop counter
choices.D: It holds the stack frame size

checkpoint.explanation: The integer argument registers begin rdi, rsi, rdx. In this function rdi is the array address, rsi is the count, and edx is the value compared with each element's id field.

checkpoint.prompt: The function begins with mov eax, -1 before it tests the count. What is the most supported reconstruction of that value?

choices.A: It is the first element's id
choices.C: It is the default return value for no match
choices.D: It is the byte offset of the flags field

checkpoint.explanation: eax is the integer return register. The early non-positive-count path goes directly to ret without changing eax, while a successful match replaces it with ecx. That supports -1 as the no-match result.

checkpoint.prompt: What property does test byte ptr [rdi], 8 check after an element's id matches?

choices.B: Whether bit 3 of that byte is set
choices.C: Whether the byte is a signed negative value

checkpoint.explanation: test performs a bitwise AND for flags and does not store a result. Mask 8 is binary 00001000, so the following je skips this element when bit 3 is clear.

checkpoint.prompt: After cmp dword ptr [rdi - 4], edx, what does jne .L5 mean for an element whose id differs from the requested value?

choices.A: Skip its flag test and advance to the next element

checkpoint.explanation: jne takes the mismatch path to .L5. That path increments the index, advances the pointer by one stride, checks the bound, and then tries the next element; the flag test is only relevant after an id match.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is rcx the best reconstruction for the loop index rather than for the return value?

choices.B: rcx always contains a pointer under System V
choices.C: It starts at zero, increments once per stride, and is copied to eax on success
choices.D: It is the third argument register

checkpoint.explanation: xor ecx, ecx initializes the counter, inc rcx advances it, and cmp rsi, rcx bounds it. On success mov eax, ecx copies that index into the ABI return register.

checkpoint.prompt: What behavior follows from test rsi, rsi followed by jle .L7 before the prologue?

choices.A: A zero count makes the loop run once
choices.B: A non-positive count returns the default value without entering the loop
choices.C: The function converts rsi to an unsigned count
choices.D: The function allocates a larger stack frame

checkpoint.explanation: The jump goes to the ret path before push rbp and before the loop setup. Since eax was already set to -1, zero and negative counts return that default without dereferencing rdi.

checkpoint.prompt: The pointer advances by 16 bytes after each unsuccessful element. What does that establish most directly?

choices.A: The array elements occupy 16 bytes each
choices.D: The flags field is 16 bits wide

checkpoint.explanation: A repeated pointer stride is the spacing between successive elements in the traversal. It establishes the element size for this access pattern; it does not reveal the array length or the return type.

checkpoint.prompt: A dword load from one field proves which limited fact about that field?

choices.A: It is definitely a signed int in the source
choices.B: It is definitely an enum in the source
choices.C: This instruction accesses four bytes at that offset
choices.D: It is the first field declared in every compatible struct

checkpoint.explanation: The size annotation gives the width used by this instruction. It does not recover the source-language type or all declarations that could share the layout; those are intent-level facts the disassembly alone does not provide.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does the positive-count path execute push rbp only after the early jle guard?

choices.A: push rbp performs the signed comparison
choices.B: The immediate-return path needs no frame setup
choices.C: The ABI forbids frames for positive counts
choices.D: The push changes rsi into the loop bound

checkpoint.explanation: The zero-or-negative path does no loop work and reaches ret directly, so it has no need to establish and later dismantle the frame. The placement is evidence for a fast early return, not a separate calling convention.

checkpoint.prompt: If two elements both match the id and have bit 3 set, which index does this function return?
checkpoint.explanation: After the first successful flag test, mov eax, ecx is followed by the shared epilogue and ret. There is no jump back to .L5 on that path, so later elements are never examined.

checkpoint.prompt: Which source-level fact remains unjustified even after this function's behavior and layout are reconstructed?

choices.A: The loop examines elements in increasing address order
choices.B: The function returns -1 on a non-positive count
choices.C: The original programmer's chosen function and field names
choices.D: The function checks an id before testing one flag bit

checkpoint.explanation: The instructions establish behavior, accesses, and control flow, but names are source-level intent. Labels can be stripped or renamed, and several source programs can compile to the same behavior, so a reconstruction should name this limit explicitly.
